title: One Ohio Town Is at the Center of a Big Data Center Debate
summary:
In the small Ohio village of Mt. Orab, farmland has become the center of a big debate about data centers. About 1,000 acres of farmland and trees were sold to a data center developer in 2024 and 2025. Building has not started yet, and no one knows when it will start.

Nick Owens, a lifelong Republican and attorney from nearby Brown County, is leading the local pushback. He says secret agreements have made it hard for people to learn details about the project. With another attorney and a real estate agent, he helped build Conserve Ohio, a volunteer group reaching nearly all of Ohio's 88 counties, with Democrats, Republicans, and independents.

This fall, the group backs votes in 10 communities to change rules and block data centers. It is collecting signatures for a constitution change that would ban them across Ohio, aiming for a 2027 vote. Supporters point to tax money, school money, and building jobs. Critics worry about secrecy, noise, pollution, and new power plants. Owens would rather use old industrial sites away from homes.
why_it_matters: Decisions about what gets built near your home can change your neighborhood, your school's money, and the land around you.

background_read: A data center is a large building full of computers that store and share information people use online.
These buildings need a lot of land and electricity, so choosing where to build one can become a big decision for a town.
In Mt. Orab, farmland was sold for a data center project, and neighbours began to argue about whether it belongs near their homes.
